subject: Covariance between exogenous variables in a mediation model

messages.author: f3807694ba8e3f19
messages.subject: Covariance between exogenous variables in a mediation model
parts:
Hi 

I'm trying to estimate a very simple longitudinal mediation model with three waves with lavaan.
I also ask the software to estimate the covariance between the two exogenous predictor from wave 1 (Esteem10 and ParInt10)
This is because it's likely that these variables are correlated with each others or they might be correlate with a third confounder (not observed) and 
I know a good way to account for this problem is to allow for them to correlate in my model.

However, from my results I got covariance estimates for ALL the exogenous variables in the model ! (even if I only asked for cov(Esteem10, ParInt10))...
Is this normal/what people should usually do? what this mean substantially? 
and ..can I leave the analysis like that and interpreting the coefficients I'm interested in (in the regression table) without this interfering with them?

Thanks a lot in advance for your help!
Ilaria


This is my syntax:

model1 <- 'Esteem_16 ~ 1 + a*ParInt10 + Esteem10 + Perform16 + OnePar16 + Female + class10 + MumEdu10
logPay ~ 1 + b*Esteem_16 + c*ParInt10 + HighEdu + OnePar16 + Female + class10 + MumEdu10
ParInt10 ~~ Esteem10
ind := a*b
total := c + (a*b)'

fit1 <- sem(model1, data = Data, missing = "ml")
summary(fit1,  standardized = TRUE)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Covariance between exogenous variables in a mediation model
parts: I got covariance estimates for ALL the exogenous variables in the model ! (even if I only asked for cov(Esteem10, ParInt10))...

sem() will do that by default, because it is a reasonable assumption that exogenous variables (i.e., variables explained outside your model) almost certainly have nonzero correlations, unless they were made to be orthogonal by design (e.g., randomly assigned treatment conditions with equal sample sizes).
Is this normal/what people should usually do? what this mean substantially?
and ..can I leave the analysis like that and interpreting the coefficients I'm interested in (in the regression table) without this interfering with them?

Yes, if you force them to be zero when their observed correlations are not zero, that will make you model fit worse.  By default, you don't even need to estimate exogenous (co)variances.  The argument fixed.x=TRUE (described on the ?lavOptions help page) means you just use the observed sample statistics in place of ML estimates of exogenous (co)variances, so it won't affect your model's df or fit.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Covariance between exogenous variables in a mediation model
parts: I understood why we should estimate the covariance of exogenous variables..but in my specific case is it not quite redundant?

Redundant with what?  Your syntax?  Yes, specifying that exogenous covariance in your model syntax would be redundant if you used the default fixed.x=TRUE because that information only needs to be taken as-is from the sample statistics.  An advantage of setting fixed.x=FALSE to estimate the exogenous parameters would be to use all available information (when using missing="fiml") if there are missing data even on the predictors.

I've put almost all of the exogenous variables in both regression analyses, and as far as I know the main "job" of regression is accounting for the covariance between predictors ( and then see if what is left influence Y)..am I right?

I think the main job of regression is predicting an outcome, not explaining relationships among the predictors.  But the predictors are allowed to be correlated even in OLS regression -- those correlations just aren't estimated.  Path analysis is more complicated because you can have not only multiple (residually correlated) outcomes but also sequences of causal effects.  So you might be interested not only in predicting each outcome, but also seeing whether outcomes still have residual correlations after accounting for shared explanatory predictors (perhaps even seeing how much of the outcomes' covariance is explained).

But these are general questions that are not specific to lavaan.  You can find more feedback for questions like this on SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html
